title: Timelag-aware kernel switcher with lightweight probing for mixed-length traffic
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Goal: reduce p95/p99 latency tails and unnecessary cost for mixed-length inference traffic by introducing a lightweight, timelag-aware kernel switching policy. Instead of relying only on static sequence-length bucketing, this ticket implements a probe-driven signal (micro-latency probes + request timelag) to pick between attention kernels and small/large-token execution paths at runtime. The approach targets live serving: minimal added overhead, quick detection of regime shifts (burst of long/short sequences), and safe fallbacks to stable kernels.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end implementation deployed to canary (1% traffic) with rollback and kill switch
Observed >=8% reduction in p99 latency on mixed-length internal traffic (synthetic + production shadow) vs baseline kernel policy, without >3% regression in token throughput
No increase in model output variance (logprob / hallucination proxies) beyond noise floor as validated on PRD prompt set
Telemetry emits events for every switch decision (reason: probe|timelag|seqlen), and dashboard charts for switch frequency and cooldown violations
Runbooks updated with safe-defaults and escalation steps
tasks: Design: define timelag metric, probe frequency, and cooldown policy (Aisha)
Spike: implement in-runtime lightweight probe microbench and simulation harness (Marco)
Integration: wire switcher into kernel selection API and prefill/decode scheduler (Marco + infra)
Testing: create synthetic mixed-length load tests and shadow traffic experiments (SRE)
Observability: add telemetry events, dashboards, and alert rules for thrashing and error rate bumps (Observability)
Rollout: canary -> 5% -> 25% with automated rollback criteria
notes: Motivation: traditional seqlen bucketing reacts slowly when traffic characteristics change rapidly (e.g., a bot flood with long prompts). Timelag (time between request arrival and decode start) correlates with queueing pressure and prefills that interact poorly with certain attention kernels. Using a short probe and timelag signal allows quicker, lower-cost decisions.

Design tradeoffs: probes add extra micro-work per candidate kernel. We limit scope: probes run only when (a) request timelag > threshold OR (b) historical switch entropy for this route > X. Otherwise fall back to cached kernel choice.
Policy: bandit-like exploration but with conservative cooldown per model variant. Default cooldown: 30s for small models, 120s for >4B models. Fail-open to baseline kernel on any probe error.
Attention kernel considerations: some attention implementations are memory-latency sensitive; the switcher prefers memory-friendly kernels under high timelag and low prefill occupancy.
Safety: versioned policy flags and per-customer opt-out for Dedicated/Private customers
